cards.title: Building a responsive homepage in Elementor (tablet/mobile pass)
cards.summary: Method for making an Elementor page builder homepage banner, product and category sections responsive across tablet and mobile by adjusting padding, direction, width and gaps.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a WooCommerce store homepage in Elementor and it looks broken on tablet or mobile breakpoints.
steps: Work section by section: select the section, open Advanced, and reduce padding (e.g. top 90, sides 20, bottom 60–90) so content isn't cramped on narrow screens.
When a banner's big heading is too large, select the text directly and lower font size (e.g. 60–64 on tablet, 36 on mobile) and line height (72 tablet, 48 mobile) separately.
For two side-by-side items that should stack, set each container width to 100% and change the parent's layout direction to column.
Add vertical breathing room with margin (e.g. margin-bottom 30 on tablet, 20 on mobile) rather than reordering widgets.
For image/illustration widgets, set a custom width (e.g. 115px, 120px, 150px) and use offset values (horizontal/vertical) instead of drag to place decorations precisely.
Adjust column gaps on the container's layout tab (e.g. gaps column 40 on tablet, gaps row 30 on mobile) to space repeated items.
caveats: Exact pixel values in the source are one designer's choices, not universal; match them to your own type scale and grid.
Gap settings sometimes don't fix a leftover gap — style the widget's margin instead (e.g. margin-right 20).
Elementor's exact panel names change between versions; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Adding more pages before theme customization
cards.summary: Create a contact page and a blog list page as standalone WordPress pages, then finish them alongside theme customization so site-wide settings apply everywhere.
cards.use_when: You have published a store homepage and now need additional pages such as contact and blog before doing global theme setup.
steps: From the WordPress dashboard go to Pages → Add New, title the page (e.g. 'Contact'), and publish.
Open the page with the page builder (Elementor) to design it.
Keep a separate 'Blogs' page as an empty placeholder: publish it, then set it under Settings → Reading as the Posts page so the theme auto-populates it with all blog posts.
Return to the homepage afterward to wire widgets (like a blog post widget) that depend on posts existing.
Expect the product grid, header and footer to remain incomplete until theme customization; treat those as the last pass.
caveats: An empty Blogs page shows content only after real posts exist.
Theme and builder menus labels may shift with updates — verify current paths.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Designing a contact page banner and contact-detail cards
cards.summary: Create a styled contact page top banner and reusable contact-detail cards (phone, email, address) using containers and icon widgets.
cards.use_when: You are building or polishing the contact page of a WooCommerce store and want it visually consistent with the brand.
steps: Add a container, rename it 'page banner', give it a background color, and set padding (e.g. 122 top/bottom, 0 sides).
Add a heading ('Contact Us'), center it, specify a large size (e.g. 72), weight 800, line height 82 and slight negative letter spacing; add a secondary intro heading below it.
If you constrain the intro text with a custom width, set align-self to center so it stays centered.
Add decorative images as absolutely positioned widgets with offset values (e.g. left 72, bottom 0) and control stacking with width and transform flip if needed.
Build contact detail 'cards' as containers: background color, border radius 12, padding 40/30. Duplicate the card three times for phone, email and shop address.
Inside each card add an icon widget (upload SVG, set view to stacked and shape to circle), then a label heading and the actual value. Reuse cards by copy/paste and only swap the icon and text.
caveats: Absolute-positioned decorative images need manual offset tweaks per breakpoint or they overlap text on mobile.
SVG upload support depends on your WordPress/plugin configuration.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Building a contact form with MetForm in Elementor
cards.summary: Assemble a styled contact form (name, email, message, submit) using the MetForm widget, then wire admin notifications.
cards.use_when: Your store contact page needs a functional form that emails submissions to you.
steps: Add the MetForm widget to the page, click Edit Form, create a new form and name it.
Inside the form builder add a container, then rows: make each row direction 'row' for side-by-side fields and adjust the column gap (e.g. 10–20px).

Add an MF Text widget for first name; turn off 'Show Label' and set the placeholder. Style padding (e.g. 17/16/17/20), text color, white background, 1px solid border, border radius ~100 for a pill shape, and set placeholder typography.
Duplicate the field for last name. Use 'Paste Style' to copy styling onto new inputs instead of restyling each.

Add an MF Email field with 'Required' enabled so the form cannot submit without it; set its width to 100%. Add an MF Text Area for message and paste the style, but reduce border radius (~20) because the large radius looks wrong on a tall box.
Add the submit widget, relabel it (e.g. 'Send Message'), align left, style padding, uppercase, accent background, radius 50%, and set box-shadow color transparent to remove default shadow.
In Form Settings → Notifications, enable admin notification, set subject, and add one or more recipient addresses separated by comma-space; save the form then update the page.
caveats: MetForm's interface differs by version; verify current label names.
Requiring email improves data quality but adds friction — consider which fields truly need to be mandatory.
Deliverability of form email depends on your host/SMTP setup.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Embedding a store location map widget
cards.summary: Add a Google Maps widget focused on your shop location by feeding the map the exact place title plus store name.
cards.use_when: Your store's contact page or footer should show where customers can find you physically.
steps: Add a Google Maps widget into a container on the contact page.
Search your shop address in Google Maps on a separate tab and copy the exact place title shown.
In the widget's location field, paste that exact title followed by a comma and your store name so the pin resolves to the right place.
Set the zoom (e.g. 13–15) so the surrounding area is visible, and set the map height (e.g. 500) to match your layout.
Add a 1px solid border with a partially transparent color and a border radius (e.g. 12) to match other cards.
On tablet/mobile, reduce the map height so it doesn't dominate the viewport.
caveats: The map only resolves correctly if the place title text matches Google's data.
A live embedded map may require an API key on some setups; confirm your configuration.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Writing and publishing store blog posts
cards.summary: Create blog posts in the WordPress block/rich-text editor with featured image, categories and tags, then surface them via a dedicated posts page.
cards.use_when: You want content marketing or SEO articles attached to your store and discoverable by visitors.
steps: From the dashboard go to Posts; trash the default 'Hello World' post and click Add Post.
Write the body in the rich text editor; use the plus icon to insert headings, lists, images, galleries, video and prebuilt patterns.
Set a Featured Image in the right-side panel — it becomes the post thumbnail wherever the post is listed.
Set the author, assign or create a Category, and add Tags.
Publish, then verify with 'View Post'.
Ensure a Blogs page exists and is assigned under Settings → Reading as the Posts page so visitors can browse all posts.
caveats: Without the Posts-page setting, visitors cannot find posts through navigation.
Comment functionality is on by default; decide whether to keep it for your store.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configuring the blog post widget on the homepage
cards.summary: Style the Elementor blog-posts widget into a clean grid of image, metadata and title for a storefront homepage blog section.
cards.use_when: You want to surface recent articles on the homepage and control exactly what each card shows.
steps: Select the blog posts widget, set the layout style to 'Grid with Thumb' and set the featured image size to full so images show at full resolution.
Turn off 'Show Content' and 'Read More' if you only want image + title cards; open Query and set number of posts shown (e.g. 3) and order by (category or recent).
Enable meta data, set position to 'Before Title', then add the meta items you want (date, author) and delete the unwanted icons.
In Style: set background type classic, make card backgrounds transparent, set box-shadow color fully transparent, and zero out radius/widths.
Style the featured image: border radius ~12, margin-bottom ~15, padding 0, and set the image to cover so corners round correctly.

Style meta typography (e.g. 14/500, line height 20) and set item margin (e.g. 10 right/bottom) with zero item padding and icon spacing; style the title (e.g. 24/600, line height 32) in your primary color.
caveats: The source notes some card layouts still need custom CSS to look right — expect to revisit.
Number of posts shown is a design choice, not a performance rule.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Setting site identity: logo, title, tagline and favicon
cards.summary: Configure WordPress site identity so the header logo, browser tab icon, site title and tagline reflect the store brand.
cards.use_when: You are doing the global brand pass on a new store and the header still shows a default site title instead of a logo.
steps: Go to Appearance → Customize → Site Identity and select your logo; choose 'Skip Cropping' to keep the full image.
Use the logo size slider (e.g. 185px) to fit the header; optionally set a retina logo for high-density screens and a separate smaller mobile logo.
Edit the site title so it describes the store (it appears in the browser tab and search results).
Write a tagline that reinforces what the store sells.
Set the site icon (favicon) and publish.
Verify the header updates immediately with the logo.
caveats: Logo dimensions vary by theme; adjust the slider until the header looks balanced rather than using a fixed number.
Retina and mobile logos are optional but help sharpness and layout on small screens.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Setting global theme layout, colors and scroll-to-top
cards.summary: Use the theme customizer's Layout and Colors panels to set a site-wide background, container width, header color, footer columns, copyright text and scroll-to-top button.
cards.use_when: You want store-wide consistency instead of fixing colors and spacing page by page.
steps: In Customize → Layout → Site Container, set the main background color every page inherits (e.g. a beige FFF0E0-type tone) and set the content width (e.g. 1240px).
Set the header background color to your accent color in the header design panel.
For blog settings, choose the blog list structure and limit how many posts load per page (source kept 20; adjust to taste).
For blog single, reorder or hide elements (title, featured image, meta) in the order you want readers to see them.
Choose where sidebars appear: e.g. sidebar on blog single and shop archive (left), but none on the blog list if you prefer a cleaner archive.

In Footer settings, set the number of widget columns (e.g. 4) and edit the copyright text; the theme supports dynamic tags like current year and site title, so remove any parts (e.g. theme author) you don't want.
Configure the scroll-to-top button: which devices show it, position (left/right), background color, icon size and border radius.
In Colors, verify theme/text/accent/link-hover colors — these propagate to buttons and many components.
caveats: Changing global theme colors affects many elements at once; preview before publishing.
Theme customizer option names vary between themes — verify in your current theme.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configuring WooCommerce catalog and product display settings
cards.summary: Tune the WooCommerce customizer panels so shop pages show the right number of products, consistent image sizes, hover behavior, sale tags and add-to-cart style.
cards.use_when: You are finishing the shop archive and need catalog, image and product-card behavior set up correctly.
steps: In Customize → WooCommerce → Site Notice, replace the default demo-store notice text or clear it once the store is live.
Under Product Catalog, set products per page (e.g. 12) — pagination appears after that count.
Under Product Images, keep the thumbnail width and cropping/aspect ratio and, most importantly, upload product images at the same width and height so cards align.
In Shop Archive → Product Content, choose what the card shows (title, rating, price) and alignment (e.g. center).
Set the product image hover effect — the source switched from gallery-image swap to zoom because the swap 'looked bad'.
For the sale tag, choose whether to show a percentage or custom text and set its background color to match your palette.
For the add-to-cart button, choose the style; the source preferred the hidden variant that appears on hover.
On Product Single, set content background, gallery layout option, and reorder description/reviews sections.
caveats: Same-size product images is a presentation rule, not a hard WooCommerce requirement, but misaligned cards hurt trust.
Hover effects and card options differ by theme/plugin version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Creating header and footer nav menus in WordPress
cards.summary: Build the primary header menu and multiple footer menus so visitors can actually navigate the store.
cards.use_when: Your store pages are published but there is no working navigation in the header or footer.
steps: In Appearance → Menus, create a new menu (e.g. 'Main Menu') and assign it to the primary/header location.
Use 'Add Items' to pull in published pages (home, shop, blog, contact); reorder them logically (e.g. shop right after home).
For the footer, create additional menus (e.g. 'Footer Menu 1' for quick links like blog/contact/shop/account) and assign them to footer locations.
Create a legal/utility footer menu (e.g. 'Footer Menu 2') with custom links for privacy policy, terms and disclaimer; use '#' as a placeholder URL until those pages exist.
Ensure each menu is assigned to a theme location, then save.
Verify navigation works from the live site, not only the dashboard.
caveats: Custom links with '#' placeholders go nowhere until you create the target pages — don't forget to fill them in.
Menu locations available depend on the active theme.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Building footer widget columns with logo, menus and contact info
cards.summary: Populate theme footer widget areas with a logo block, descriptive text, navigation menu blocks and contact details.
cards.use_when: The footer area is empty and you want quick links, brand identity and contact details there.
steps: Go to Appearance → Widgets and add a Columns block (one column) into the footer widget area.
Add an Image block for the store logo; in the block's settings set a width (e.g. 200px) so it isn't oversized.
Add a Paragraph block after the image with a short brand description.
In the next footer column add a Navigation Menu block, give it a title (e.g. 'Quick Links') and select the corresponding footer menu.
Repeat for additional footer menus (e.g. a 'Website' column for legal links).
Add a Heading block ('Contact Us') plus contact detail blocks in a final column.
Because the footer column count is set in the theme customizer (e.g. 4 columns), match the number of widget columns you populate.
caveats: Footer widget areas must be registered by your theme; missing areas mean you must use a footer builder instead.
Block editor vs widget editor differences will shift some labels — verify in your WordPress version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Catching left-over homepage sections and finishing the pass
cards.summary: Recognize which homepage sections (e.g. blog grid, product grids) remain incomplete and defer them until their dependent content or global setup exists.
cards.use_when: You are finishing a store homepage and some sections look broken or empty.
steps: Identify sections that depend on content not yet created — a blog section is empty until posts exist and a posts page is set.
Identify sections that depend on global customization — product grids and button styles may be fixed via theme-level CSS or customizer settings rather than per-widget tweaks.
After creating the missing content, refresh the page and re-select the widget to surface its settings.
Log the remaining fixes (header setup, footer setup, product settings) and address them in the customization phase rather than forcing them early.
Publish and re-check the homepage end to end.
caveats: The source explicitly defers some visual fixes to custom CSS in the customization phase; don't assume every issue is a widget setting.
